‘Imran wants movement for his release expedited’. • Dr Uzma says Imran being denied ‘human interaction’; suffering from anxiety, fears dying in isolation ‘like Egypt’s Morsi’ • Pims statement says eye doctors from Shifa participated in PTI founder’s medical check-up ISLAMABAD: Fearing that he will be ‘killed th­­r­ough isolation’, PTI foun­der Imran Khan has cal­led on Khyber Pakhtun­k­hwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi to expedite the movement for his release, Dr Uzma Khan said on Friday after a brief meeting with her brother during his checkup at Pims in the early hours. Addressing a press conference alongside her sisters and PTI leaders, Dr Uzma said that her bro­ther had complained that he was not allowed any human interaction, which he described as a form of ‘mental torture’. She said that her bro­th­­er was suffering from an­­xiety, and feared the same end as former Egyptian ruler Mohamed Morsi. Imran was not aware of anything, especially current developments, as he does not have access to ne­­­wspapers or television for the past 10 months, she said. In response to a query about his he­­alth, she said he was “fit”, with no­­rmal blood pressure and imp­roved vision. “Just a small haemorrhage is left,” she added. However, she quo­ted her brother as saying that a doctor who examined him on Aug 10 said that he had severe anxiety due to “mental torture in solitary confinement”, and that anxiety caused high blood pressure. Dr Uzma added that Imran said when he would complain about his health to prison doctors, “no one would listen or care”. Narrating what he had told her, Dr Uzma said Imran Khan had asked her to request KP CM Afridi to expedite the movement for his release. Consequently, the PTI-led opposition alliance announced its plans to hold a full-fledged protest on Sept 27. Separately, PTI Cent­ral Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram also assailed the government for defying SC ord­ers, say­­­ing: “Declaring the PTI founder medically fit after a few hours of what appe­ars to have been a merely symbolic exercise and then shifting him back to Adiala jail before dawn raises serious questions”. However, in a late-night statement, the administr­ation of the Pakistan Ins­titute of Medical Sciences (Pims) said that two specialists from Shifa Inter­national Hospital participated in Mr Khan’s eye assessment, while other exa­minations were carri­­ed out by the concerned Pims specialists. “The clinical input ari­sing from the ophthalmological assessment was taken into account alongside findings of the investigations conducted at Pims,” the statement said. PTI lawmaker not allowed to speak on ‘SC order violation’. ISLAMABAD: The Senate session was adjourned on Friday without transacting any business minutes after the chair disallowed a PTI lawmaker from raising the issue of non-compliance with Supreme Court orders on shifting former prime minister Imran Khan from Adiala jail to a private hospital in the federal capital. Senator Manzoor Kakar was in the chair when Senator Mishal Khan Yousafzai sought to speak during the Question Hour. Despite clear court directions, Imran Khan was not taken to Shifa International Hospital, Senator Yousafzai said, while regretting that he was taken to PIMS instead and rushed back to prison within a short span of time. “If the government cannot implement the Supreme Court’s decision, we will not let the House run,” she declared. Calling attention notice on Pak-Iran gas pipeline among agenda items not taken up “You should speak on Question Hour for now,” the chair told her, and did not allow further discussion on the matter. Following the exchange, Senator Mishal pointed out the lack of quorum in the House, and the chair ordered the bells to be rung. However, quorum could not be completed despite the calls, with the result that the proceedings had to be adjourned till Monday evening. Among the items listed on the agenda that could not be taken up were two calling attention notices including the one related to Pakistan-Iran Gas pipeline. Senator Muhammad Talha Mahmood was supposed to draw the attention of the Minister for Energy (Petroleum Division) to the non-completion of the Pak-Iran Gas Pipeline within Pakistan, which he said was resulting in a consistent gas shortage in the country. Also, Senator Zeeshan Khanzada was expected to raise the issue of shortage of essential drugs due to delays in price approval/notification by the government, leading to the supply of spurious medicines in the market. The House was also scheduled to take up the motion of thanks, moved by Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Dr Tariq Fazal Chaudhry on May 8, expressing “deep gratitude to the President of Pakistan for his address to both Houses assembled together on 2nd March, 2026.” Published in Dawn, August 22nd, 2026

PM admonishes commissioner, IGP over display of ‘pomp and show’. ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has taken a serious exception to the display of “pomp and show” and “personal aggrandisement” by the top city managers during the Independence Day parade in Islamabad , directing them to ensure that such conduct does not recur. In a formal advisory, Establishment Division Joint Secretary (Discipline) Syeda Shafaq Hashmi conveyed the Prime Minister’s displeasure to Islamabad Inspector General of Police Syed Ali Nasir Rizvi and Chief Commissioner Sohail Ashraf over their appearance in a ceremonial horse-drawn buggy during the August 14 celebrations. The advisory, addressed separately to the IGP and CDA chairman, said the prime minister had taken a “very serious view” of the incident at the official function held on August 14, when the two senior officials rode in a ceremonial horse-drawn buggy, attracting widespread public criticism. According to the document, the prime minister expressed “deep disappointment and displeasure” at the display of pomp and show, observing that it projected an image of “privilege, ostentation and personal aggrandisement” that was at odds with the ethos of public service. Both turned up at Independence Day event in buggy The prime minister stressed that civil servants and public functionaries should demonstrate humility, restraint, dignity and sound judgment at all times. Such conduct, he observed, undermined public confidence in public institutions and was inconsistent with the standards expected of senior civil servants and government officials. The advisory further reminded the officials that, as administrators of the federal capital, they were expected to uphold the highest standards of propriety, conduct and responsible governance. “You are advised to be careful in the performance of your duties, and ensure that such conduct should not recur,” the advisory stated, adding that it should be treated as an instruction for “strict compliance in letter and spirit”. The prime minister’s reprimand comes days after a video of the two officials riding into the Independence Day parade in what appeared to be the presidential buggy went viral on social media. The footage showed Mr Rizvi and Mr Ashraf arriving in the horse carriage while the gathering was apparently prompted to applaud. However, no applause could be heard in the widely circulated clip. The spectacle drew criticism online, with some users describing it as reminiscent of a colonial-era display of authority and privilege. The episode, however, received a different interpretation from Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who defended the two officials. In a statement on X, Mr Naqvi said the officials were not at fault, explaining that the chief guest and he had been delayed due to a meeting between the president and prime minister. As the public had been waiting since 5pm, he said, the officials were instructed to commence the programme around 6pm rather than keep the crowd waiting. According to the minister, the horse carriage had originally been arranged for the chief guest but had to be used by the officers because of “unavoidable circumstances”. He said both officials had initially resisted starting the programme in the absence of the chief guest and the minister but proceeded only after being specifically instructed to do so for the convenience of the public. Crime Control Department constable held responsible for death of Australian girl in Chakwal. CHAKWAL: An inquiry into the killing of nine-year-old Australian national Hania Ahmed has found a Crime Control Department (CCD) Punjab constable guilty, concluding that he opened indiscriminate fire on a car without prior permission from senior officers. The incident took place on the night of June 10-11 outside the CCD police station in Chakwal city. Adeel Ahmed, an Australian national, his wife and two minor children were being robbed by two armed men when the constable fired at Adeel’s car. Hania was killed, while both Adeel and his son Afan were injured. On June 18, CCD Chief Additional IG Sohail Zafar Chatha and Punjab Police IG Abdul Karim told a joint press conference in Lahore that the inquiry would be completed within a week. However, the report was submitted to the prosecutor’s office as a challan on July 28. The 200-page report, obtained by Dawn , said the investigation was conducted by CCD Chakwal Sub-Inspector Muhammad Irfan. According to the report, the accused constable stated that he was standing near the main gate of the CCD police station when he heard noise outside. He said he saw two armed men robbing a white car at the western corner of the station. “On seeing me, one armed person fired at me with a pistol and I also fired towards the robbers,” he stated. “To save myself from the firing I took cover behind a wall. Meanwhile, the car sped away towards Islamia Chowk and I took a lift on a private motorcycle and went after the car but could not find the car.” However, Duty Officer Inspector Jahanzeb Khan rejected the constable’s version. He told investigators that the constable fired from the official SMG without permission from him or any senior officer and chased the car on a private motorcycle, also without permission. Three other officials present at the station at the time corroborated Inspector Khan’s statement. The inquiry declared the constable’s claim of acting in private defence “completely wrong and contrary to facts”. It noted that 14 pistol bullet casings and 13 Kalashnikov casings were recovered from the scene. Thirty-four witnesses were included in the report. One of them, Ahmed Nawaz of Mohalla Circular Road, said he knew the constable. He told investigators he was returning home after offering a funeral prayer at nearby Sarpak Ground when he reached the CCD police station and saw the constable standing outside with a Kalashnikov. “He fired 12 to 14 shots one after another at a car going ahead,” Ahmed Nawaz stated. He later learnt that the family in the car was related to him. The report added that a final opinion from the Punjab Forensic Science Agency regarding the bullets that hit Hania, Adeel and Afan, and the blood samples, has not yet been received. A police officer said that due to court holidays in August, the formal trial was expected to begin in September. Published in Dawn, August 22nd, 2026

Hospital visit. ALL the government had to do was take a prisoner from jail to an appointed hospital and allow them to have their medical tests administered under the supervision of individuals they trust. This would have checked off the directive issued by the Supreme Court some 48 hours earlier, and earned the PML-N some much-needed goodwill. Instead, it took an adversarial stance against the order, insisted on having its own way despite explicit directions from the court, delayed implementation till the very end, and then failed to implement the order in a letter while claiming that it had fulfilled its ‘technical’ requirement. To what end? As the drama unfolded on Pakistani news media on Friday, the government itself was helping cement the perception that the jailed former prime minister, Imran Khan, remains as relevant as ever. It turned a routine matter into a high-stakes political crisis. This, of course, was not the first time this government has insisted on its own interpretation of court orders despite clear instructions to the contrary. And it appears that the other side, too, has started discounting the power and privileges of the judiciary. Despite clear prohibitions on ‘politicising’ Mr Khan’s health issues as a condition to meet him, the sister who met the PTI founder, Dr Uzma Khan, promptly held a very public media briefing on Friday afternoon, detailing her interaction with the jailed leader and the health issues he had complained to her about. The court had warned it would withdraw the relief it had granted Mr Khan if his family or lawyers went public about his health, but it seems they gave short shrift to the condition after seeing yet another order flouted with impunity. As a result, the Supreme Court was made to look irrelevant by both parties, who turned it into a political tussle. The government, specifically the PML-N, appears intent on keeping Mr Khan behind bars and away from the public eye. The flustered reaction which various ministers and allied talking heads had to the Supreme Court order exposed a level of insecurity that no amount of grandstanding can cover up. At a time when the state apparatus is rumoured to be gearing up for major legislative changes, and when a key coalition partner is rallying the opposition to thwart the government’s legislative agenda and force concessions out of it, the PML-N has come out of this episode looking weak. With a little bit of magnanimity, it could have easily tided over the Supreme Court’s intervention without losing any political capital. It can still make amends. There is no harm in allowing prisoners access to medical facilities of their choosing. With concerns rising over the welfare of political prisoners, especially women incarcerated for unprecedented periods by this government, it can still choose magnanimity over retribution. The beneficiaries of war. WARS are generally assessed through a binary lens. Strategic analysts, policymakers and the media tend to focus on a simple question — who won and who lost? The recent US-Iran war has generated a similar debate. Has Washington been able to achieve its objectives? Has Iran successfully withstood American military pressure and preserved its capacity to resist? But this binary framework overlooks another, often more consequential, dimension of modern warfare. Wars do not merely produce military winners and losers. They also redistribute wealth, accelerate technological change and create commercial opportunities for industries positioned to profit from insecurity. In the case of the US-Iran conflict, the most obvious beneficiaries may ultimately be neither Washington nor Tehran. The two capitals have both paid a substantial price. They have expended military resources, suffered economic disruption and experienced varying degrees of tactical and strategic pain. The conflict may therefore produce no clear geopolitical victor. Yet several sectors have emerged as unmistakable commercial winners. The foremost beneficiary of the US-Iran conflict has been the defence industry. Modern wars consume extraordinary quantities of missiles, interceptors, drones, precision-guided munitions and other military equipment. Every missile fired has to be replaced. Every depleted stockpile creates new procurement requirements. Every perceived vulnerability generates pressure for additional defence spending. The financial results of major US defence companies illustrate this dynamic. Several sectors have emerged as unmistakable commercial winners in the US-Iran conflict. Lockheed Martin reported earnings of $1.8 billion in the second quarter of 2026, compared with $342 million during the same period in 2025. Its sales increased by 11 per cent to $20.1bn, while its backlog reached a record $230bn. Sales in its missiles and fire control segment increased by 19pc to $4.1bn. Similarly, RTX, the parent company of Raytheon, reported Q2 2026 net income of $2.139bn, up from $1.657bn in the corresponding quarter of 2025. Raytheon sales increased by 18pc to $8.269bn, supported by demand for systems such as Patriot, Standard Missile and AMRAAM. A prolonged conflict not only increases the immediate consumption of weapons but also generates a second wave of demand, ie, replenishment of stockpiles. The conflict between the US and Iran has resultantly become a multi-year procurement cycle for these firms. The longer the insecurity persists, the more governments feel compelled to order additional weapons, ammunition and defensive systems. For the military-industrial complex, geopolitical instability can translate into expanding order books. Select firms in the energy sector have been another major beneficiary. The US-Iran war, combined with uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz and disruptions to regional energy flows, created precisely the conditions in which large oil companies, refiners and commodity traders tend to thrive on higher prices, supply uncertainty and extreme market volatility. The figures are striking. ExxonMobil’s Q2 2026 net income reached $14.5bn, compared with $7.08bn in the corresponding period of 2025, which is an increase of almost 105 pc. Similarly, Chevron’s earnings increased dramatically, while Marathon Petroleum, Phillips 66 and Valero Energy also recorded major gains as higher energy prices and refining margins transformed geopolitical disruption into exceptional financial returns. The trend was not confined to the US. Shell reported Q2 2026 profits of $9.84bn, compared with $4.26bn in Q2 2025, while British Petroleum reported $5.7bn, compared with $2.34bn during the corresponding period. TotalEnergies, Saudi Aramco, Glencore and Trafigura also benefited from the extraordinary volatility created by the conflict and the resulting disruption in energy markets. The point is not that every energy company automatically benefits from every war. Conflict can also destroy infrastructure, disrupt production and create substantial risks. But the US-Iran war demonstrates how supply disruptions and uncertainty can produce extraordinary gains for companies capable of trading volatility, refining crude and exploiting higher prices. For many firms, instability itself can become profitable. The beneficiaries of modern conflict are no longer limited to companies manufacturing tanks and missiles. Warfare is increasingly dependent on artificial intelligence, cloud computing, satellite data, cybersecurity and real-time battlefield analysis. Palantir Technologies has emerged as one of the glaring examples of this transformation. In Q2 2026, the company generated revenue of $1.94bn, representing 93pc year-on-year growth. Revenue from the US government reached $809m, an increase of 90pc. Microsoft also secured a five-year Pentagon contract worth $9.69bn for Microsoft 365, cloud subscriptions and other services for the US military and intelligence community. At the same time, the Pentagon has been pushing AI companies to expand their capabilities into classified networks, creating new opportunities for firms capable of developing secure AI systems for military and intelligence purposes. The US-Iran war may therefore accelerate a structural transformation in the military marketplace. Global shipping industry is another example of war-generated profits. Disruption of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz forced vessels to alter routes and created enormous uncertainty in global shipping markets. The resulting increase in freight rates transformed tanker operations into a highly profitable business. Frontline and Scorpio Tankers are some prominent examples with record Q1 and Q2 earnings of 2026. There are also less visible beneficiaries. Defence consultants, geopolitical risk firms, intelligence service providers, private security contractors and an expanding ecosystem of digital media personalities have all found that geopolitical crises generate unprecedented demand for their products, services and content. Although, decisions on war and peace are determined by governments, it is equally difficult to ignore the political economy associated with prolonged warfare. This raises an uncomfortable question: if war creates exponential profits for some industries, would they prefer the settlement of conflicts or their prolonged continuation? The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own. X: @itskhurramabbas Published in Dawn, August 22nd, 2026

Dynamics of reorganisation. WHILE debating the question of carving out more ‘administrative units’ from Pakistan’s existing four provinces, we may find it relevant to study how India has reorganised its states (equivalent to our provinces) since independence. The example is pertinent because of the shared circumstances of the two countries created out of undivided India. They inherited the same interim constitution — the Government of India Act, 1935 — which each adapted to fit its own context. Both countries chose a parliamentary form of government. Pakistan adopted a more explicit federal character, while India shied away from calling itself a federation. Instead, it opted to describe itself as a ‘union with some federal characteristics’. Probably, India’s more diluted form of federalism helped it carve an uncomplicated path for creating new provinces: a simple majority in parliament and a non-binding consultation with the concerned states. On the other hand, Pakistan’s 1973 Constitution made the creation of new provinces contingent upon the passage of a resolution in the concerned provincial assembly or assemblies by a two-thirds majority before the bill for new provinces could be tabled in parliament and passed in the two Houses by a two-thirds majority. This set the bar very high for altering the boundaries of the provinces as compared to India. Around the time of Partition, undivided India consisted of 14 provinces and 587 princely states, of which two provinces (Bengal and Punjab) were partitioned. Both India and Pakistan received a part of each province. Three provinces — Sindh, the North-West Frontier Province (now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) and British Balochistan — joined Pakistan, taking the tally of provinces in India and Pakistan to 11 and five respectively. Thirteen princely states acceded to Pakistan. The rest either voluntarily acceded to India or were coerced into doing so through brute military force. Kashmir has remained a disputed territory ever since. The reorganisation of Indian states was triggered by language riots after a political activist, who had been demanding a separate state from Madras for Telugu-speaking people, died in 1952 following a fast unto death. When the riots spread, the Government of India fast-tracked the creation of the Telugu-speaking Andhra state (later called Andhra Pradesh) out of Madras state. The demands for more states based on language spread. The Indian government constituted a three-member States Reorganisation Commission in December 1953, headed by a former judge of the supreme court. As Pakistan debates new provinces, India’s experience offers relevant insights. The commission, constituted to propose the redrawing of state boundaries, also came to be known as the Justice Fazal Ali Commission after the chairman. Its proceedings continued for about 21 months and it submitted its report in September 1955. Parliament finally passed the States Reorganisation Act in 1956, leading to the redrawing of boundaries and the creation of 14 states and six union territories. Language was a major consideration but not the only one in the creation of the states. The creation of the new states continued even after the enactment of the States Reorganisation Act. Four years later, Bombay state was split into the Gujarati-speaking Gujarat state and the Marathi-speaking Maharashtra. After persistent demands by the tribes, Nagaland was carved out of Assam state in 1963 because of its distinct language and culture. Indian Punjab was split into three parts, with Punjabi-speaking Punjab, Hindi-speaking Haryana and the hilly northern tracts merged into Himachal. In all, 15 new states were created or upgraded from union territories after the enactment of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. In the meantime, some areas were downgraded to union territories; the latest such move saw the illegal splitting of Indian-occupied Jammu and Kashmir into the two ‘union territories’ of Ladakh and Jammu & Kashmir in 2019. The latest tally is 28 states and eight union territories. As stated earlier, most of the new states and union territories were created on the basis of identity such as language, ethnicity, culture and geography, or the difference in the level of development in two parts of a state. There is hardly a case where a state was created just because of its large population. Uttar Pradesh, with an estimated population of over 243 million, is a case in point. The state’s population almost matches the population of Pakistan. The population of the US has increased 10 times since 1863, but not a single state has been carved out of the existing ones since then. The last state created this way was West Virginia, which had seceded from Virginia in 1863 during the Civil War. What are the lessons from the two-country case studies above? The first is that population on its own is not enough of a reason to split a province into two or more units. Pakistan’s population has increased four times since 1973, but this alone may not justify the creation of more provinces. There may be merit in the proposal to create more provinces, but such reorganisation should be studied in depth, preferably by a commission or even a parliamentary committee as was done when the 18th Constitutional Amendment was being drafted. The concentration of too many powers in the provinces is a key issue that needs to be addressed. Creating more provinces may not be the best solution for this problem as it will not only be an expensive exercise but may also create political instability in one or more provinces. The problem, in my opinion, may be solved by creating a balance of powers among the three tiers of the state — federal, provincial and local. This balance can be effectively achieved by empowering local government through a comprehensive constitutional amendment, as India did in 1993. The LGs already have elaborate infrastructure and staff, unlike the proposed new provinces. The proposed amendment should not only guarantee adequate powers for various tiers of local government but should also ensure the direct transfer of funds to LGs from the National Finance Commission. The writer is president of the Pakistan-based think tank Pildat. president@pildat.org X: @ABMPildat Published in Dawn, August 22nd, 2026

Maryam fires a fresh salvo at PPP, PTI. LAHORE: Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz on Friday fired a fresh salvo at coalition partner Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), accusing it of corruption and warning political rivals against targeting her government’s performance. “One party (PPP) is involved in corruption and the other (PTI) in anarchy. I would like to ask them to follow in the footsteps of the PML-N to serve the people,” Maryam said while speaking at the inauguration of a cardiac transplant centre at the Jinnah Institute of Cardiology here on Friday. The chief minister’s remarks appear to signal a hardening of PML-N’s stance towards the PPP, which has recently intensified its criticism of the federal and Punjab governments over their political mandate and alleged electoral irregularities in Azad Kashmir. The latest exchange has exposed growing strains within the ruling alliance, with PPP leaders repeatedly describing the PML-N governments as products of a “Form-47 mandate”, while PML-N leaders have increasingly hit back by questioning the PPP’s record of governance. Ms Nawaz’s cabinet members, particularly Punjab Information Minister Azma Bokhari, have already been engaged in a war of words with the PPP, mainly over the latter’s criticism of the Punjab government’s performance and its references to Form-47 following the Kashmir elections. On Friday, CM Maryam herself entered the fray, making it clear that her government would respond if the PPP continued to target the PML-N, particularly over its governance in Punjab. Earlier, Ms Bokhari had accused the PPP of being unable to “digest” the pace of development in Punjab under Ms Maryam’s administration. “Those who are envious of Punjab’s progress and prosperity may continue to criticise, but the journey of public service will not stop,” Bokhari had said. The PPP, however, has maintained that the PML-N lacks the moral authority to question its governance or political standing. Sindh Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon recently accused the PML-N of having come to power on the basis of a “ fake mandate ”. “The public knows who came to power through Form-47 and who enjoys the real mandate. The PML-N has been pursuing politics marked by arrogance, intolerance and provocative rhetoric,” he said. The PPP’s criticism echoes a central allegation made by Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) since the Feb 8, 2024 general elections — that the election results were manipulated to deprive the party of seats and facilitate the formation of PML-N-led governments. The increasingly sharp rhetoric between the two coalition partners comes despite their continued political cooperation at the federal level. The exchanges suggest that while the two parties remain allies in government, their political interests — particularly in Punjab and Sindh — are becoming increasingly difficult to reconcile. Reading Thucydides in the wolf world. The term Thucydides’s Trap has caught on since Professor Graham Allison wrote his 2017 book, Destined for War: Can America and China Escape Thucydides’s Trap? The core concept comes from Greek soldier-historian Thucydides’s History of the Peloponnesian War who identifies the structural stress that occurs when a major rising power is perceived to threaten to displace an established power. My intention here is not to explain Allison’s work or his treatment of the trap but to point to how modern-day scholars and policymakers cherrypick episodes from Thucydides’s work to justify their own approaches. I believe, as the post-World War II international security architecture unravels and we enter what some describe as the wolf world, that it is important to analyse Thucydides’s history in view of the book’s hermeneutics rather than picking up episodes that suit one’s own predilections. Thucydides arrived in the United States policy corridors with Dr Henry Kissinger. He had taught the text at Harvard and was keenly familiar with it. But upon joining Richard Nixon’s administration in the White House, he sought fit to focus on the Melian Dialogue, colouring outside the lines. The one line, “The strong exact what they can; the weak concede what they must,” became the slogan of Cold War strategies. Kissinger knew that Thucydides message was far more nuanced and he was not justifying imperial overreach. But that was for the classroom. The world Kissinger had to tackle was one in which ‘man was wolf to man,’ homo homini lupus of Plautus popularised by Thomas Hobbes. That misrepresentation has generally informed US policymakers since then. Now that cruder minds are ruling America and the precepts of International Law, for whatever they were worth, have been defenestrated and America’s foreign policy has become a Kabuki theatre, a few words about Thucydides’s work are in order. The structural architecture of History of the Peloponnesian War relies on a psychological arc that connects the Plague of Athens, the Melian Dialogue (nearly 14 years later) and the Sicilian Expedition (a year later). Far from putting down a simple chronicle of military manoeuvres, Thucydides tracks the internal rot of the Athenian psyche through the description of the Plague. By tracing this trajectory, the reader discovers that the moral dissolution initiated by the plague directly fostered the intellectual hubris that were to lead to Melos, which inevitably culminated in the material ruin of the Sicilian campaign. The foundational fracture occurs in Book Two with the Plague (430 BCE). Thucydides describes a city where the sudden, indiscriminate terror of death obliterates law ( nomos ) and religious restraint. Faced with immediate mortality, citizens abandon honour for instant gratification, arguing that the virtuous and the wicked die alike. This lawlessness ( anomia ) institutionalises a new societal ethos: the abandonment of traditional justice in favour of self-interest and survival. The plague does not merely kill bodies; it extinguishes the moral constraints of the polis. Might and appetite replace civic virtue. The plague, Thucydides tells us, also claimed Pericles and his family. That death, within the hermeneutics of the text, becomes a metaphor for the demise of nomos. The emergence of more populist and aggressive figures, such as Cleon, who prioritised personal popularity and raw emotion over steady strategy, comes to symbolise anomia. This internalised lawlessness manifests later as aggressive foreign policy in the Melian Dialogue (416 BCE) of Book Five. But the seeds of Melos were sown earlier. Two years after Pericles’ death, Athens had the Mytilenian debate between Cleon and Diodotus. Cleon fiercely argued in favour of executing the entire population of Mytilene to send a message of terror. While Diodotus narrowly persuaded the assembly to reverse the decision to execute all citizens, the Athenians still exacted a brutal and bloody punishment on the city. At Melos, the Athenian envoys articulate a chilling political realism, famously declaring that, “the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.” This worldview seems to be the direct philosophical descendant of the plague’s nihilism. Having lost their respect for divine law and cosmic justice during the pestilence, the Athenians now claim that the rule of the stronger is a universal law of nature. The moral decay hardened into intellectual hubris. Athens no longer seeks to justify its empire through justice or leadership, but purely through raw, unyielding power. The immediate narrative pivot to the Sicilian Expedition (415–413 BCE) in Book Six reveals this hubris in action, dramatised through the opposing speeches of Nicias and Alcibiades. Nicias represents the ghost of old Athenian moderation. He desperately warns the assembly against overreach, cautioning that they are leaving enemies behind to chase a massive, unknown island. But the plague-damaged psyche of Athens, now driven entirely by imperial appetite and the illusion of invincibility, cannot tolerate restraint. Instead, they rally behind Alcibiades (notice the shift from the Cleon-Diodotus debate). Alcibiades is brilliant, reckless, and entirely devoid of civic responsibility. He appeals to the city’s insatiable desire for expansion, arguing that an empire must grow or it will wither. Ultimately, Thucydides’s narrative acts as a tragic warning. The lawlessness born in the plague pits became the strategic blindness that was to mock the Melians and finally drove Athens to sail into the Sicilian trap. In Sicily, the inversion is completed. The Athenians are utterly destroyed, reduced to the same desperate reliance on “hope” and suffering that they had ridiculed at Melos. Through this connection Thucydides demonstrates that the real danger of power overreach is not always external opposition but the internal erosion of the moral and intellectual clarity required to understand the limits of power. There are no perfect analogies but history’s verdicts are often uncannily similar. Header image: An AI-generated bust of Henry Kissinger in the likeness of Thucydides.

US judge strikes down policy suspending immigrant visa processing for 75 nations, including Pakistan. A US judge on Friday struck down a Trump administration policy suspending the issuance of immigrant visas to applicants from 75 countries, including Pakistan, saying that the policy exceeded Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s statutory authority. US District Judge Jeannette Vargas in Manhattan said the policy that the State Department announced in January was “patently unlawful” and ran afoul of federal immigration law, which explicitly stripped the secretary of state of authority over consular officers’ processing of immigrant visas. “The policy, which categorically prohibits the issuance of immigrant visas based upon the nationality of the applicant, represents a direct abrogation of this statutory scheme,” she wrote. The State Department’s suspension that also took effect in January impacted applicants from Latin American countries including Brazil, Colombia, and Uruguay; Balkan nations such as Bosnia and Albania; South Asian countries Pakistan and Bangladesh; and those from many nations in Africa, the Middle East, and the Caribbean. The State Department said applicants from those countries were “at a high risk for becoming a public charge and recourse to local, state and federal government resources in the United States”. The department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling. Vargas, an appointee of Democratic former President Joe Biden, issued the ruling in a lawsuit filed by immigrant rights groups Catholic Legal Immigration Network and African Communities Together along with applicants for immigrant visas and US citizens who are sponsoring family members from the designated countries for immigrant visas. US President Donald Trump has pursued an aggressive immigration crackdown that he says is aimed at improving domestic security. Rights groups ⁠say ​the crackdown has violated free speech and due ​process rights and has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised ​concerns about racial profiling.

US hits Canadian goods with 50pc tariffs after trade talks fail. The United States imposed 50 per cent tariffs on some ‌Canadian goods on Saturday after the two longstanding allies failed to reach a trade deal, with each side accusing the other of derailing days of talks. The tariffs that came into effect just after midnight (0400 GMT) on some $20 billion of Canadian goods — things like wooden ice hockey sticks that are rarely used anymore — are far ​from an economic game-changer for the largest US trading partner after Mexico. That represents just over 5pc of Canada’s exports to ​the US. But the new tariffs mark an increase in tensions between President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney, ⁠and will likely make broader talks to renew the US-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement more difficult. Carney said he had suspended trade negotiations and ​Canada would retaliate “dollar for dollar” on the new tariffs. “I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the US and have directed Canada’s negotiators to ​return to Ottawa,” Carney said in a statement. “They (negotiators) have worked hard, in good faith, to defend the interests of Canadians throughout these negotiations up until the very last minute,” he said. “However, last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.” Carney, the only person to ​ever run the central banks of two major economies, was elected last year on promises to stand up to Trump, and remains broadly ​popular. Polls show most Canadians oppose making any concessions to Trump. Hours earlier, the two sides had seemed close to an agreement that sources said would have ‌lowered ⁠tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos and potentially brought American alcohol back to Canadian liquor stores. “Tonight, Canada declined to finalise the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week,” US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said during a White House briefing. “This is a missed opportunity for Canada to partner with the United States, which is the fastest-growing economy in the G7,” Greer said. A senior Trump administration official said the US offer ​would have put Canada in the ​best tariff position of any ⁠major exporter to the US, but that Canada had sought additional concessions, especially on steel, aluminum, autos and softwood lumber. No additional talks are scheduled as the US implements the new duties, the official said. Trump last month ​threatened to impose a raft of duties on a range of Canadian imports including wine, furniture, ​dairy products, cement, clothing, ⁠fishing rods, hockey equipment. The tariffs, which do not qualify for preferential treatment under the US-Mexico-Canada free-trade agreement, open up some already vulnerable sectors to potential severe damage that could lead to job losses and business closures, trade experts have said. The decision by the US administration followed three days of ⁠talks in ​Washington between Canada’s minister for trade with the US, Dominic LeBlanc, and Greer. The new ​duties add to existing US tariffs on steel, lumber and autos which have taken major hit in the last 18 months, although the malaise has been largely contained within ​these sectors.

Indonesia and China discuss increasing defense cooperation and energy security. JAKARTA, Indonesia (AP) — Top ministers for Indonesia and China agreed during meetings in Jakarta on Friday to increase their defense cooperation and strengthen food and energy security. The meetings come as Jakarta deepens military ties with China while trying to maintain its long-standing non-aligned foreign policy and balance relations with other major powers. China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi said Indonesia and China agreed to better coordinate on their top development and security priorities as the two countries modernize. Wang said the dialogue will “send a clear signal to the world of solidarity and cooperation between our two major emerging-market countries.” Indonesian Foreign Minister Sugiono said the two sides discussed strengthening food, energy and mineral security through the development of industries that support national resilience, which in the future will encompass areas such as artificial intelligence, the joint development of communications satellites and other advanced technology initiatives. “We also agreed to facilitate trade, including market exploration and the expansion of market access for Indonesia’s flagship commodities,” Sugiono, who uses one name, said in a jointly released statement. The countries’ defense ministers, Indonesia’s Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin and China’s Dong Jun, met separately and discussed intensifying defense cooperation. “We also invite the Chinese armed forces to participate in joint exercises, such as the Heping Garuda exercise, which is a concrete example of the relationship between the Indonesian National Armed Forces and the Chinese armed forces,” Sjamsoeddin said. He added that Indonesia and China will collaborate on a joint munitions factory in Indonesia, which will also produce missiles and rockets. China will transfer technology to Indonesia as part of the plan, which is set to begin in 2027. Indonesia’s economic ties with China have flourished in recent years, reaching about $167 billion in 2025. China has become Indonesia’s largest trading partner and plowed billions into major infrastructure projects such as the Jakarta-Bandung high-speed railway and Cirata, Southeast Asia’s largest floating solar power project, on a reservoir in West Java, 130 kilometers (80 miles) from the capital, Jakarta. Disagreements have emerged over the pricing and timing for the projects, but China says it is determined to follow through on them in keeping with President Xi Jinping’s signature “Belt and Road” initiative to build infrastructure throughout the region.

Video games, violence, and very angry comments. FILLER Ban violent video games, a lawmaker says. Ban Netflix, another senator adds. Ban social media, still many others suggest. But very few seem to want to check on the state of the Filipino family. Fewer still highlight the kind of role models people have today. Go figure. This is not going to be a defense of violent video games or films, of course. Regulation in this area exists, although it can perhaps be improved. It is, nevertheless, there. Instead, this is an attempt to understand why certain individuals have shown a rather limited understanding of—or an even more limited attempt to understand—the problem at hand, and requires immediate action and attention. As such, I will not delve into a possible explanation of why school shootings happen. Instead, I will comment on those who have been very loud about their proposed measures to solve the issue. To ban carte blanche any form of media that has violence in it, or any that purportedly promotes it, is an oversimplified band-aid solution. Should this be the direction taken, any public figure that has the slightest tinge of violence in his or her public persona should also be banned. Further, paraphrasing one artista’s comment, if supposed violent video games are to blame, then there should have been an earlier generation of school shooters in the Philippines (those that grew up on first-person shooter games played on LAN in computer shops, i.e. my generation). Yet there were none. So why are people quick to throw the blame on video games? The long and short of it is this: It is laziness. It is a kind of laziness to pinpoint and address the real source of the problem, simply being content with adding some noise to the discussion in an attempt to appear relevant, all the while harping on people’s heightened emotions. This approach is not new when it comes to solving the nation’s problem. Some of those in public service, not all of them but a good number of them, are used to providing band-aid solutions. One only needs to look at the state of public roads and highways to see this. There’s a crack on the road? Apply a layer of asphalt and you’re good to go. Problem solved, at least until the next floods come. Throw almost any problem at the government (past and present), and they solve it with ayuda. Typhoons are coming? Ayuda. Floods devastate towns. Ayuda. Oh maybe the world throws a pandemic curveball? Ayuda. Do you have a relative who died because of lack of access to decent healthcare? Ayuda. Ayuda culture, for one, is the most glorified of these temporary fixes. It has become such a feature of how public service is carried out that for many Filipinos it is probably what they consider to be public service. Following this logic, the best politician is the one who doles out help when needed. If you check who has been topping elections in recent decades, you would see how this has been the way Pinoys judge whom to put in positions of power. The rush to ban video games is itself an example of the country’s preference for quick, visible solutions over difficult structural ones. To be sure, there are other services being provided by those in government out there. But these are rarely highlighted, partly because it is not what people easily understand—not because they can’t, but because those in power have made sure that people want ayuda more than any solution. After all, who doesn’t want a quick solution? Ayuda, unfortunately, is the least helpful solution of all. It is the band-aid solution to all band-aid solutions. It creates a culture of contentment, both in the minds of the public and in those of public servants. Instead of getting fixated on what they truly deserve—a really comprehensive and effective healthcare system, improved transportation infrastructure, better access to education and job opportunities, to name a few—they become content with getting scraps (some cash aid here, a pack of goods and bigas there, and a pat on the back for resilience). And for those in public service, cultivating a culture of ayuda is a cheat code for winning in the next elections and staying in power. To build a true healthy society, there is no such thing as a quick fix, unfortunately. When Filipinos start asking for what they truly deserve, then maybe public servants would not settle for just quick fixes. Maybe, instead of asking for banning violent video games and media, they would start looking at the state of Filipino families to identify the real cause of the recent shooting incidents.

Old and new tech. HOTSPOT I’m writing this on my phone using a keyboard that’s like more than 15 years old or maybe years older. I can’t remember now how I got it, where I bought it, and for how much. What’s important right now is that it still works like a charm. Old, aging technology is still technology. One wouldn’t readily know from interactions online what phone they use. Even if they say that they use iPhones, we wouldn’t know if one’s using an iPhone 11 or a brand-new 2TB iPhone 17 Pro Max paid in cash. Of course, those who use the latter are most prone to “flaunting” their device for all the world to know that they spent a ₱100,000 for a phone. They both still work, backed by Apple’s security updates and app updates from vendors. The same is true with Android smartphones. We wouldn’t be able to easily guess which brand a person uses. American tech bloggers and vloggers regularly churn out content that ask “would this piece of tech from five or 10 years ago still work?” I’m pretty sure hundreds of millions of people worldwide know the answer. Outside of the US, and even in parts of the US, the overwhelming majority of people use “old” or “aging” smartphones. The second-hand phone market is worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The problem is that American tech bloggers and vloggers have come to believe and preach that every year when Apple or Samsung introduces new models of the iPhone or the S series, the old model becomes somewhat “obsolete.” It is as if the old model stops working or can no longer fully function as a smartphone. They help Apple and Samsung sell the brand-new models that way. And so when you visit YouTube, you will encounter videos of Americans marveling at how “old” iPhones still work. Of course, they do! It is not impossible that these “tech experts” don’t know that Apple continues to support iPhone models for many years with software and security updates. Here in the Philippines, there are certainly a number of Filipinos who upgrade to the new iPhones every year. We see many lining up for hours or days in the lead up to the midnight launch events. But whether there’s tens of millions of iPhone 17 users right now, that cannot be true. The stingy telcos still have stocks, as well as the authorized resellers. It defies logic to expect a majority working-class nation to be a majority iPhone 17 country, especially how expensive the phones are and the proliferation of much cheaper Androids. According to multiple sources, the most-used iPhone models are still the iPhone 11, 12 and 13. Yes, old models. But phones that still work for every conceivable purpose. No new bells and whistles, and no non-monumental changes found in the iPhone 17, but the old phones still work, still supported, still could post, do ChatGPT, and so on. Some would argue that devices from the past were once touted as future-proof, and so they find that out for themselves. That’s something good for the planet and for their wallet. In fact, the second-hand market for tech devices is quite popular in the Philippines. Titos and titas, and other elders who are in the know (most probably younger GenX and senior millennials) would advise Gen Zs to opt for previously-owned high-end phones and laptops instead of buying brand-new but cheap lower-end models that tend to be disposable, not upgradable and have a lot of limitations like having relatively-ancient components. The truly ancient tech right now are the Pentiums (circa 1993) and Celerons (circa 1998) from Intel, and the Symbian, Palm and WindowsPhone OS. Which is why there was an uproar when it was found that a government agency acquired during the pandemic el-cheapo Celeron laptops at high-end prices. Today, the cutting-edge tech have AMD processors, and the latest OS from Apple and Android. Prices are expected to rise because of a global memory-chip shortage. More people may choose not to upgrade or get priced out by new, more expensive tech. Apple has in fact said that price increases are inevitable. Whether for school, for work, or for personal use, we are bound to grapple with tech options. Second-hand or new. Entry-level or bleeding-edge. Mac or Windows. Apple or Android. We thus have to read and be informed so we could get the “best bang for the buck”, so to speak. Here, Filipino tech bloggers and vloggers should be able to help.

From bright ideas to patents: Government must back young innovators. NIGHT OWL Young people are often told that they are the future, yet many governments still ask them to build that future with little more than enthusiasm. A student may develop a water-saving device, a low-cost medical tool, a new software platform, or a cleaner production method, but the journey from idea to protected invention is expensive, technical and intimidating. If governments genuinely want innovation-driven economies, they must support young inventors from the first sketch to the final patent. The first step is to make innovation education practical and available. Schools, colleges and community centers should offer laboratories, maker spaces, coding facilities and design workshops where young people can test ideas without having to purchase costly equipment. Innovation should not be treated as an activity reserved for elite universities. A teenager in a rural town should have the same opportunity to prototype an invention as a student in a city. Government support must then move beyond competitions and certificates. Too many youth innovation programmes celebrate winners on a stage but leave them alone afterward. What young inventors need is a clear development pathway: technical mentoring, business guidance, legal advice, prototype funding, product testing and access to potential manufacturers. Every publicly funded innovation competition should include at least a year of structured follow-up support for promising projects. Funding is important. Small grants can make the difference between an idea that remains in a notebook and one that becomes a working prototype. Governments should create youth innovation funds with simple applications, fast decisions and transparent criteria. Grants should cover materials, software, laboratory fees, certification, market research and patent-related costs. Young applicants should not be excluded because they lack collateral, a registered company or an established financial history. Patenting deserves special attention because the intellectual property system is difficult to navigate. Patent searches, technical drawings, legal drafting and filing fees can be beyond the reach of students and first-time inventors. Governments should establish patent support desks in universities, technical colleges and regional enterprise centres. These desks could provide free preliminary patent searches, confidential consultations and referrals to qualified patent professionals. A national patent voucher scheme would help. Eligible young inventors could receive government-funded vouchers to pay for professional drafting, filing and examination costs. Support should continue through international patent applications when an invention has strong export potential. Without this assistance, young people risk disclosing their ideas publicly, losing ownership, or signing unfair agreements with better-resourced partners. Protection alone, however, is not enough. Governments should help inventors turn patents into products. Public procurement programmes could reserve opportunities for youth-led innovations that solve problems in health, agriculture, education, transport and environmental management. Incubators should connect inventors with manufacturers, investors and entrepreneurs. Patent offices, standards agencies and funding bodies should work together rather than sending young innovators from one institution to another. Accountability is essential. Governments should publish data showing how many young people receive support, how many prototypes are completed, how many patents are filed and granted, and how many inventions reach the market. Programmes should also ensure equal access for young women, people with disabilities, rural communities and low-income families. Supporting young innovators is not charity. It is an investment in new jobs, competitiveness and national problem-solving capacity. A government that funds education but abandons young people at the point of invention wastes talent and public money. The goal should be a complete innovation pipeline: inspire, train, fund, protect, produce and scale. When young people know that a good idea can receive support all the way to patenting and commercialization, they are more likely to take risks, solve local problems and create the industries of tomorrow.

You have found favor with God. REFLECTIONS TODAY The feast of the Queenship of the Blessed Virgin Mary, instituted by Pope Pius XII in 1954, honors Mary not only as the Mother of God but also as our Queen, reigning with Christ in glory. This feast draws inspiration from Scriptures. The book of Revelation speaks of “a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars” (12:1). This image fittingly illustrates Mary, the mother of the Messiah, now gloriously crowned in heaven. In his Letter to the Romans, Paul writes about God’s purpose and predestination, reminding us of Mary’s unique role in salvation history (8:28-30). The Gospel, in turn, points not to a grand lady, but to a humble handmaid of the Lord who obeys his bidding. But because the Lord looks upon her lowliness, people of all ages will call her blessed (Lk 1:48). Mary’s queenship, as all her other states and privileges, is intimately associated with Jesus. As Jesus’ kingship is marked by his being the Good Shepherd, Mary’s queenship is characterized by maternal care that embraces all her children, especially those in need. She is our advocate, our sweetness, and our hope. She listens to our prayers, comforts us in our sorrows, and leads us to her Son. Just as she interceded for the bride and groom at the wedding feast in Cana, she is present in our lives, interceding for us before her Son, Jesus. First Reading • Is 9:1-6 [or Ez 43:1-7ab] The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; upon those who dwelt in the land of gloom a light has shone. You have brought them abundant joy and great rejoicing, as they rejoice before you as at the harvest, as people make merry when dividing spoils. For the yoke that burdened them, the pole on their shoulder, and the rod of their taskmaster you have smashed, as on the day of Midian. For every boot that tramped in battle, every cloak rolled in blood, will be burned as fuel for flames. For a child is born to us, a son is given us; upon his shoulder dominion rests. They name him Wonder-Counselor, God-Hero, Father-Forever, Prince of Peace. His dominion is vast and forever peaceful, from David’s throne, and over his kingdom, which he confirms and sustains by judgment and justice, both now and forever. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this! Responsorial Psalm • Ps 113 [or 85] “Blessed be the name of the Lord for ever.” or “Alleluia.” Gospel • Lk 1:26-38 [or Mt 23:1-12] The angel Gabriel was sent from God to a town of Galilee called Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man named Joseph, of the house of David, and the virgin’s name was Mary. And coming to her, he said, “Hail, full of grace! The Lord is with you.” But she was greatly troubled at what was said and pondered what sort of greeting this might be. Then the angel said to her, “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall name him Jesus. He will be great and will be called Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will rule over the house of Jacob forever, and of his Kingdom there will be no end.” But Mary said to the angel, “How can this be, since I have no relations with a man?” And the angel said to her in reply, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God. And behold, Elizabeth, your relative, has also conceived a son in her old age, and this is the sixth month for her who was called barren; for nothing will be impossible for God.” Mary said, “Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord. May it be done to me according to your word.” Then the angel departed from her.
